Amazon blames DNS misconfiguration for hours-long AWS outage

Published 2026-10-07 14:10 UTC

Amazon has published a preliminary explanation of Wednesday's AWS outage: an automated DNS update left the endpoint for DynamoDB in the US-EAST-1 region resolving to an empty record. Services that depend on DynamoDB, including EC2 and Lambda, began failing, and the outage spread to customer apps such as Slack, Venmo, Ring and Fortnite.

AWS engineers corrected the DNS record within about two hours, but the full recovery took nearly seven hours because of throttled EC2 launches and a large backlog of queued requests in northern Virginia.

Amazon says it has disabled the automation that made the change and will add safeguards before re-enabling it. Critics point out that many companies still run critical systems only in US-EAST-1, so a failure in one AWS region can take a large part of the internet offline.

According to Amazon's preliminary summary, a routine change to the internal DNS configuration for a core database service introduced an error that caused other services to stop resolving the addresses they needed. Automated recovery systems made the problem worse by repeatedly retrying failed requests, which overloaded parts of the network.

Engineers rolled back the change within about an hour, but recovery took much longer because services had to restart in a specific order and clear their backlogs. Amazon said some customers saw elevated error rates for up to six hours, mostly in services that queue work for later processing.

Amazon said it will add safeguards to its configuration deployment system, including additional validation and a slower rollout process for changes to DNS records. It will also improve the isolation between services so that a failure in one does not spread as widely, and it promised a full post-event summary.

Reliability engineers said the incident follows a familiar pattern: a small change in a foundational system, followed by cascading failures and retry storms. They noted that DNS has been involved in major outages at several cloud providers and content delivery networks, partly because so many systems depend on it and its failures are hard to diagnose quickly.

The AWS outage in the US-EAST-1 region, in northern Virginia, knocked Slack, Venmo, Ring doorbells and Fortnite offline for hours, and Amazon Web Services status updates showed increased error rates and latencies across many services before the DNS misconfiguration was rolled back.

Amazon Web Services is down for many customers during the outage: Slack messages failed, Venmo payments stalled and Ring alerts stopped while US-EAST-1 services returned errors. Amazon said engineers applied mitigations, worked through backlogs and that all services in the region recovered by the afternoon.
